newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Asian refineries under pressure to cut output.
newsitem.headline: Asian refineries under pressure to cut output.

text.p: The scorching bull run in crude oil prices is leaving oil product prices in its wake and has placed pressure on Asian refineries to cut production once again.
Refineries said they expect weak profit margins on refining -- the difference between crude input prices and product output prices -- through to the end of the year.
This is despite the fact that the fourth quarter is one of the biggest demand periods of the year for middle distillate products such as gas oil (diesel) and jet/kerosene.
"If product prices in December do not rise to maintain the margins, refineries will be under pressure," one crude trader said.
Malaysian Tapis crude oil -- the benchmark crude for middle distillates production in Asia -- is valued at $26.50 per barrel, just below the five year high of $26.68 seen on October 21.
Dubai, another crude used heavily by Asian refineries, is valued at $22.35 -- just under its five-year high of $22.37 reached on October 15.
Singapore gas oil is valued at $30.20 per barrel and kerosene at $30.10 per barrel, but traders say the margin over crude is not enough to ensure profits when the cost of production is included.
"It does not make sense to run your refinery hard," said one trader for a refinery.
Singapore refiners, who produce 1.2 million barrels per day (bpd) of oil products, cut runs in June and July because of weak profits.
South Korean refiners prefer to maintain market share than maximise profits. Thailand's refiners are also facing weak margins and have cut production in recent months to improve economics.

Currently, traders said the most basic refinery operations were negative for most grades of crude oil. More complex processes are producing fluctuations in margins from less than $1.00 to several dollars in profit.
One trader said, "I don't think they (complex margins) are negative, but they are not very good."
The dilemma facing refineries for the rest of the year is that petroleum product prices are also at very high levels.
Gas oil hit a five-year high of $30.65 on October 16. Fuel oil did the same on October 9 at $124.00 per tonne.

But crude prices have also hit five-year highs, but then continued to rise. They have not surpassed levels reached during the Gulf War, but have risen enough to hurt profitability, crude traders said.

"It's a matter of who makes the sacrifice," said one trader, referring to refineries cutting back production to improve their profits. "It will take a brave man to cut production when it's one of the hottest markets for distillates," he said.
But another trader took a less sanguine view.
"If everyone is facing the same economics, then everyone would cut runs," he said.
